# The Explanation of the Noble Sutra of the Four Dharmas

Homage to <term>Manjushri Kumara</term> <gloss>the youthful Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>.

Why was this sutra, which states, "A Bodhisattva, a great being, should not abandon these four dharmas even for the sake of their life as long as they live," composed? It was composed to correctly instruct those who are confused about the methods for attaining unsurpassed enlightenment, even though they have entered the Great Vehicle <term>Mahayana</term>; to cause those who are heedless to correctly uphold [the teachings]; to correctly uplift those who are discouraged; and to cause those who have correctly entered [the path] to be truly joyful.

The number "four" is mentioned to avoid excessive length, so that those who do not wish to listen to such things may be avoided. Mentioning the number also allows for easy recollection. The patience and gentleness that appear later are not distinct, as they serve the same purpose.

Although there are many categories for those who have entered the Great Vehicle, two names are mentioned for three reasons: through aspiration, through application, and through realization. What is meant by aspiration? One is a "Bodhisattva" because one aspires to the profound objects of knowledge. One is a "great being" (<term>mahasattva</term>) because one aspires to great power. What is meant by application? It is because one strives for unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment for oneself, and because one strives to fully protect all sentient beings from suffering. What is meant by realization? It is because enlightenment is realized through two powers. What are the two? They are the power of wisdom and the power of diligence. Without wisdom and with little diligence, one cannot realize enlightenment. As long as one lives,

<margin>Poison exists even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is forced to admit this. If this is therefore true, I now ask you whether poison should not be separated from the good and useful, and the good accepted, while the evil is left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I ask you to explain to me how this is separated in your workshops? For among you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted to admit that poison lies hidden there, and you are asked where it eventually goes, you then bring forth I know not what about "corrections," which supposedly extract and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is ventilated.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or after Diagridium <note>a purgative preparation of scammony</note>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it gone?
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test this, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know that not sluggishly. Thus you also correct Turbith <note>a purgative root</note>, and call it Diaturbith. Such are your corrections, which would befit rustics and should be given to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see whether you will not feel the poison.
<margin>What "to correct" means for a physician.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* Whoever is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who has been punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; it is situated with them, not with you. Now, in this case, the physician must consider nothing more than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without any harm. The same must be understood equally regarding all other things, namely, that a similar separation is necessary. That not having been done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your place, or the greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will remain.

Now, therefore, if that true foundation is necessary which removes the poison, how does Alchemy provide it? For it is necessary that this be done in such a way that, if Mars <note>iron</note> is in the Sun <note>gold</note>, Mars is removed, and if Saturn <note>lead</note> is in Venus <note>copper</note>, it is separated from it. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist in them. But as for the bodies that are contrary, it is necessary that some of them be entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is removed, and the evil which you seek is taken away from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so much less useful is medicine that does not pass through fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into another generation, which ought to conduce to and assist man. And should this not deservedly be considered the proper foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to apply poisons, but true secrets.

And although it may not be perceived by smell, is one therefore allowed to say that the stench has been separated and no longer remains? Indeed, it is present, but corrected by fumigation.
